title: Complex discharge: a medication + follow-up checklist improves adherence
vignette: A 75-year-old woman is hospitalized for a bowel obstruction related to adhesions from previous uterine cancer surgery and radiation. She has a history of hypertension, atrial fibrillation, and peripheral vascular disease. After a prolonged hospital course complicated by a pulmonary embolus, she is discharged on multiple medications, including a higher dose of her warfarin. The patient is scheduled for follow-up appointments with her internist, gynecologist, cardiologist, and gastroenterologist. She lives by herself and has been able to successfully manage her care needs in the past. Her adult daughter is supportive but lives out of state. Which of the following interventions would be most effective in improving her adherence to outpatient treatment?

clues.text: discharged on multiple medications, including a higher dose of her warfarin
clues.note: A complex, CHANGED medication regimen (e.g., a new warfarin dose) is a major source of post-discharge errors - a written checklist reduces this risk.

clues.text: follow-up appointments with her internist, gynecologist, cardiologist, and gastroenterologist
clues.note: Multiple follow-up appointments across specialties create a complex schedule that a checklist helps the patient track.

clues.text: lives by herself and has been able to successfully manage her care needs in the past
clues.note: She is independent and capable, so an individualized tool she can use herself (a checklist) is more effective than relying on others.

whatMatters: For a capable but complex patient facing many medications (including a changed warfarin dose) and multiple specialist follow-ups, the most effective adherence aid is a DISCHARGE CHECKLIST listing her medications (purpose, dose, schedule) and follow-up appointments. Written, individualized instructions reduce medication errors and missed appointments better than verbal reminders. Answer D.
strategy: Pick the concrete, patient-centered tool that addresses BOTH complexity sources (medications + appointments) for an independent patient. A written checklist beats verbal emphasis (easily forgotten), sending summaries to specialists (helps providers, not the patient's self-management), giving a technical hospital-course copy (confusing), or relying on the out-of-state daughter (not present to help daily).

options.text: Emphasize the importance of adherence to treatment during the discharge process
Ensure that the discharge summary is sent to all outpatient specialists
Provide the patient with a detailed copy of her hospital course
Provide the patient with a checklist to keep track of her medications and follow-up appointments
Review discharge instructions with the patient's daughter

eliminations.label: Verbal emphasis - easily forgotten
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: stressing the importance of adherence verbally. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: patients are often overwhelmed by verbal information at discharge; a written, specific checklist is retained and acted on far better. ✅ Correct if: reinforcing a simple single instruction, not managing a complex regimen.

eliminations.label: Send discharge summary to specialists - helps providers, not self-management
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: forwarding the discharge summary to outpatient providers. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it improves provider communication but does not help the PATIENT track her own medications/appointments (the adherence question). ✅ Correct if: coordinating care between providers.

eliminations.label: Detailed hospital-course copy - technical, confusing
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: giving the patient a copy of the physician's hospital course. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is written in technical language and doesn't organize her medications/follow-ups into an actionable plan. ✅ Correct if: documentation for records/providers, not patient self-management.

eliminations.label: Review instructions with the daughter - out of state, not present daily
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: relying on the daughter to help. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the daughter lives OUT OF STATE and isn't available for day-to-day medication/appointment management; the independent patient needs her own tool. ✅ Correct if: the patient depended on an on-site caregiver for medications/transport.

reasoning: Capable but independent patient with a complex, changed medication regimen and multiple specialist follow-ups
Post-discharge errors arise from medication complexity and fragmented follow-up
A written, individualized checklist of medications + appointments directly targets both and is usable by her
-> provide a medication and follow-up checklist; answer D
mechanism: The transition from hospital to outpatient care is a high-risk period for adverse events and avoidable readmissions, especially with multiple medical problems, COMPLEX medication regimens (including dose changes such as a new warfarin dose), low health literacy, and fragmented follow-up. The most effective strategy is a structured, patient-centered DISCHARGE CHECKLIST that lists medications (their purpose, dosing schedule, and adverse effects), clearly flags medication CHANGES made during the hospitalization, and enumerates follow-up appointments, pending tests, and whom to call. Written at an appropriate literacy level, such a checklist gives the patient a concrete tool to organize and adhere to a complex plan - reducing medication errors and missed appointments - and is superior to verbal reminders (easily forgotten), technical documents, provider-to-provider summaries (which don't aid the patient's self-management), or reliance on an out-of-state relative. Because this patient is independent and previously self-managed successfully, an individualized checklist best supports her adherence.
